If $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \amp 2 \\ 2 \amp 1 \\ \end{bmatrix} $, then there is an orthogonal basis of eigenvectors $\vvec_1 = \twovec11$ and $\vvec_2 = \twovec{-1}1$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_1=3$ and $\lambda_2=-1$. Using these eigenvectors, we form the orthogonal matrix $Q$ consisting of eigenvectors and the diagonal matrix $D$, where $$Q = \begin{bmatrix} 1/\sqrt{2} \amp -1/\sqrt{2} \\ 1/\sqrt{2} \amp 1/\sqrt{2} \end{bmatrix},\hspace{24pt} D = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \amp 0 \\ 0 \amp - 1 \end{bmatrix}. $$ Then we have $A = QDQ^T$.

Notice that the matrix transformation represented by $Q$ is a $45^\circ$ rotation while that represented by $Q^T=Q^{-1}$ is a $-45^\circ$ rotation. Therefore, if we multiply a vector $\xvec$ by $A$, we can decompose the multiplication as $$ A\xvec = Q(D(Q^T\xvec)). $$ That is, we first rotate $\xvec$ by $-45^\circ$, then apply the diagonal matrix $D$, which stretches and reflects, and finally rotate by $45^\circ$. We may visualize this factorization as in [fig-diag-factors].

The transformation defined by $A=QDQ^T$ can be interpreted as a sequence of geometric transformations: $Q^T$ rotates by $-45^\circ$, $D$ stretches and reflects, and $Q$ rotates by $45^\circ$.

$$\stackrel{Q^T}{\longrightarrow}$$

$$ D \\ \swarrow \\ $$

$$\stackrel{Q}{\longrightarrow}$$

In fact, a similar picture holds any time the matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable.
